newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian banks seen rivals to term lenders.
newsitem.headline: Indian banks seen rivals to term lenders.

text.p: The entry of Indian commercial banks into term-lending spells lean times for financial institutions unless they radically alter their fund-raising strategy, the Prime Broking Company said on Monday.
So far only the State Bank of India has entered the term-lending market but other banks are scouting for opportunities.

Financial institutions' profitability would suffer unless they diversified their income streams and obtained access to funds from retail markets to meet the competition from banks, a study by the Bombay-based securities firm said.
Banks had lower costs of funds, enabling them to undercut financial institutions in some recent instances, Prime said.

"Easy liquidity coupled with sluggish demand for term financing has resulted in a rate war in the market. If the rate war intensifies we could see the already thin spreads of financial institutions coming down to negligible levels."
Prime said financial institutions were slow in responding to the challenge.
"None of them has yet set in place an organisation or system for deposit or retail fund mobilisation."

The first steps to enable market-making in bonds issued by a financial institution have been initiated by the Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) It was too early to evaluate its success, Prime said.
India's leading institutions are the IDBI, the Industrial Credit and Investment Corp of India (ICICI) and the Industrial Finance Corp of India (IFCI)
"As far as improving investor communication and transparency of accounts are concerned, the financial institutions have a long way to go," Prime analyst Amit Rajpal said in the study.

Excess liquidity caused by repeated cuts in banks' cash reserve requirements and sluggish demand for bank credit had had a negative influence on financial institutions in the short and medium term, the Prime study said.
The financial institutions have raised over 20 billion rupees through public debt issues in the first half of 1996/97 (April-March) at costs ranging between 17.0-18.0 percent.
Only part of these funds could be disbursed in the first half, the rest having been deployed in short-term instruments.
"With the recent fall in the rates of short-term instruments, the 'holding cost' of the money has shot up, impacting short-term profitability negatively," Prime said.
Borrowers are demanding lower rates for long-term money, affecting fresh loan sanctions and medium-term profits.
Indian financial institutions reported a 31 percent fall in loan sanctions in the first half of 1996/97 mainly due to recessionary conditions in commodity markets and high lending rates.
"We see this slowdown in sanctions affecting disbursements moderately in the second half of FY1997 (April-March) and dramatically in the first half of FY1998," Prime said.
It said financial institutions were suffering a knock-on effect from India's policy of liberalisation, which had hurt some some sectors of the economy and reduced their ability to borrow.
